section_summary: This section documents the aftermath, domestic causes, and international ramifications of the February 26 Incident (the 1936 military coup d'état) in Tokyo, in which rebel army officers assassinated senior statesmen. It encompasses press clippings and diplomatic despatches from Tokyo, Dairen, Tsingtao, Shanghai, and Lisbon detailing the pacification of the revolt, the death of police defenders, the escape of Prime Minister Okada, the establishment of a special court-martial under martial law, and the composition of the successor Hirota Cabinet. Comprehensive analyses by Ambassador Joseph C. Grew and State Department officials explore the deeper socio-economic unrest, zaibatsu influence, constitutional controversies, military factionalism, and the political fallout of the February 20 Diet election that culminated in the uprising.

subfiles.about: Newspaper clippings from The Japan Advertiser and The Japan Times reporting on rebel casualties, police victims, the establishment of a special military tribunal, and Prime Minister Okada's escape.
subfiles.summary: Clippings cover Nonaka's suicide, rebel imprisonment, police casualty lists, a special court-martial ordinance, and Okada's secretary's account of hiding while his look-alike was killed before Okada escaped disguised.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1721 (Enclosures): Press Clippings on the February 26 Incident and Aftermath

subfiles.about: Consular report summarizing a conversation between South Manchuria Railway President Yosuke Matsuoka and the Soviet Consul at Dairen concerning the Tokyo uprising.
subfiles.summary: Dairen reports Matsuoka telling Soviet Consul Golubtsov the rebellion targeted capitalism and corruption, not the Emperor, comparing it to overthrowing the Shogunate and expressing confidence imperial princes could control the military.
subfiles.title: Consulate Dairen Despatch: Statements of Mr. Y. Matsuoka in Regard to Attempted Military Coup d'État in Tokyo
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo

subfiles.about: Consular report on the calm reaction of the local Japanese resident community in Tsingtao to the Tokyo military uprising.
subfiles.summary: Sokobin reports the coup caused no disturbance among Tsingtao's 15,000 Japanese residents, who called it an effort to end tolerance of the Minobe theory and cleanse parties.
subfiles.title: Consulate Tsingtao Despatch: Reactions Among Local Japanese to Tokyo Coup
subfiles.to: Nelson Trusler Johnson, American Ambassador, Peiping

subfiles.about: Comprehensive diplomatic report by Ambassador Joseph C. Grew analyzing the underlying and immediate causes of the February 26 military insurrection, enclosing an interview with Dr. James A. B. Scherer.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew provides a detailed assessment of the fundamental causes of the February 26 Incident, pointing to post-World War I mental unrest, severe economic distress among farmers contrasted with corporate zaibatsu wealth, the Minobe constitutional controversy regarding imperial prerogatives, and misinterpretations of the 1882 Imperial Rescript that encouraged direct action over military discipline. He identifies immediate triggers as the scheduled transfer of the 1st Division to Manchuria, the court-martial of Lieutenant Colonel Saburo Aizawa for the murder of General Tetsuzan Nagata, and the military's frustration over the Minseito victory in the Diet election. The despatch encloses a memorandum of conversation between Embassy officers and Dr. James A. B. Scherer, who articulated the radical anti-capitalist ideology of General Jinzaburo Mazaki's faction, depicting the young officers as desperate patriots resisting plutocratic domination.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1718: An Analysis of the Causes Leading to the Incident of February 26, 1936

subfiles.about: Despatch transmitting and comparing official condolence messages and communications exchanged between the American and British embassies and the Japanese Foreign Ministry.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew compares American and British diplomatic notes prompted by the February 26 assassinations, observing that Secretary of State Cordell Hull wisely avoided specific labels while British Ambassador Sir Robert Clive explicitly condemned the deaths at the hands of 'assassins' and later congratulated the Japanese government on peacefully ending the revolt. Enclosed are Hull's note of condolence, Grew's letter expressing gratitude to Foreign Minister Koki Hirota for the protective guard placed around the American Embassy, Clive's formal messages, and Hirota's official reply conveying profound thanks for American sympathy.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1719: Messages of Condolence on Recent Assassinations in Tokyo

subfiles.about: Despatch evaluating the February 20 Diet election and its role in precipitating the February 26 coup, preceded by a State Department summary memorandum.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Preceded by a State Department briefing memorandum by Wallace T. Turner summarizing the election for the Under Secretary, Ambassador Grew's despatch analyzes the outcome of the general parliamentary election of February 20, 1936. The election resulted in significant gains for the moderate Minseito and the proletarian Shakai Taishuto, while dealing a severe defeat to the opposition Seiyukai and unseating its leader, Dr. Kisaburo Suzuki. Grew concludes that the military extremists, realizing the election had consolidated support for the moderate Okada administration, grew desperate and resorted to armed insurrection six days later to forcibly destroy the cabinet and senior statesmen bloc.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1706: The Diet Election of February 20, 1936, and Its Bearing on the Uprising of February 26, 1936

subfiles.about: Memorandum of conversation between Under Secretary William Phillips and Japanese Ambassador Hirosi Saito regarding the prospective appointment of Foreign Minister Arita and the domestic political crisis.
subfiles.from: William Phillips, Under Secretary of State
subfiles.summary: Phillips records Saito saying Arita would likely become Foreign Minister and calling the crisis a burst boil likely followed by calm.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation with the Japanese Ambassador

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum analyzing the February 26 coup, the military's influence on cabinet formation, and the policy program of the new Hirota administration, with circular transmittal instructions.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: This document, submitted by Stanley K. Hornbeck, contains a comprehensive Division of Far Eastern Affairs study examining the February 26 coup and the formation of Prime Minister Koki Hirota's non-party cabinet. The study explains that while the army disciplined the mutineers and purged factional leaders like Generals Mazaki and Araki, War Minister General Juichi Terauchi demanded major policy concessions, including increased military appropriations, rural economic relief, and stronger continental diplomacy toward China and the Soviet Union. The document includes a full roster of cabinet appointees and copies of circular instructions dated March 23 transmitting the memorandum to the American ambassadors in Tokyo and Peiping.
subfiles.title: Department of State Memorandum: The Coup and the Formation and Composition of the New Cabinet

subfiles.about: Despatch reporting on Portuguese press editorial commentary regarding Japanese expansionism and the Tokyo military rebellion.
subfiles.from: Robert Granville Caldwell, American Minister, Lisbon
subfiles.summary: A Lisbon paper sympathetically framed Japan as a bulwark against Bolshevism and Chinese disorder, calling the February 26 rebellion genuine patriotism for Japan's survival.
subfiles.title: Legation Lisbon Despatch No. 873: Portuguese Comment on Japanese Policy in the Far East

subfiles.about: Document file note and excerpted report quoting editorial reactions from major British newspapers regarding the February 26 assassinations and rebellion in Tokyo.
subfiles.from: Ray Atherton, American Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, London
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: London despatch reproduces British press (Guardian, Telegraph, Times) alarm over Japanese militarism, comparing it to Nazism and warning of regional danger.
subfiles.title: Document File Note and London Report: The Tokyo Murders (British Press Comment)

subfiles.about: Despatch transmitting a consular review and press editorials from Shanghai regarding Chinese, foreign, and Japanese reactions to the February 26 Incident.
subfiles.from: Clarence E. Gauss, American Consul General, Shanghai
keywords: The Shanghai Evening Post and Mercury
subfiles.summary: Consul General Clarence E. Gauss transmits a copy of his despatch No. 52 to Ambassador Nelson T. Johnson in Peiping, summarizing reaction in Shanghai to the Tokyo rebellion. Gauss reports that despite efforts by Japanese Ambassador Hachiro Arita to downplay policy changes, Chinese observers feared increased military domination and aggression, while foreign observers noted with concern the Japanese tendency to condone patriotic violence. Enclosures include editorial analyses from British and American publications, such as Oriental Affairs and The Shanghai Evening Post and Mercury, examining the pathological fanaticism of the young officers and its origins in the courtroom handling of Lieutenant Colonel Aizawa's court-martial.
subfiles.title: Consulate General Shanghai Despatch: Sino-Japanese Relations: Shanghai Opinion on February 26 Incident
